tldr: Instead of leaping away with large whole-body motions, humanoid robots can evade incoming projectiles through quick, localized adjustments like pulling an arm back or lifting a leg. This paper proposes "BARE," a reflexive evasion framework that performs rapid local evasion while recovering posture without falling.
hero_caption: Diverse evasive behaviors demonstrated by a Unitree G1 robot powered by BARE against objects flying from various directions and heights. The robot executes localized bodily adjustments based on the threatened region, such as crouching, ducking, leaning back, raising an arm, or lifting a leg.
overview:
When robots share spaces with humans, sudden hazards like flying balls or unexpected obstacles are inevitable. Conventional walking path planning and footstep adjustment take too long from perception to execution, making it difficult to dodge fast-moving objects approaching from close range. While dynamic reflexive evasion—such as jumping far sideways—has been studied in quadruped robots, applying the same tactic to humanoids poses a high risk of falling upon landing and risks collisions with nearby walls or furniture in confined spaces.

To tackle this, the researchers focused on the rich articulation unique to humanoids. Much like a human ducking their head, pulling an arm back, or lifting a leg slightly to dodge a flying object, "local evasion" minimizes displacement and enables much faster reaction times. However, rapid movements of the arms or legs shift the center of mass, introducing a new challenge: how to avoid toppling over.

To solve this issue, the team proposed "BARE" (Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion). Leveraging human evasive motion data, BARE predicts when and where an incoming projectile will hit at the individual link level, selects an optimal reference motion, and stretches or compresses its playback speed to match the collision timing. Furthermore, a reinforcement learning policy coordinates local body adjustments while maintaining whole-body balance.

Through simulations and real-world experiments on a Unitree G1, BARE achieved a higher avoidance success rate than baseline methods even with very short arrival times, while dramatically reducing power consumption and base movement distance.
contributions: Formulated dynamic obstacle avoidance for humanoids as a risk-conditioned reflexive control problem that balances local evasion of threatened body regions with whole-body stability, rather than relying on whole-body repositioning.

Proposed a risk-guided motion adapter that selects an appropriate motion from a human evasive motion library based on link-level collision risk and adapts its temporal phase according to collision urgency.
Constructed a residual reinforcement learning policy that leverages human reference motions while achieving both targeted evasion of threatened regions and whole-body stabilization and recovery.
Demonstrated reflexive evasion and posture recovery against attacks from multiple directions and heights using both simulation and a real Unitree G1 humanoid robot.

sections.heading: Why do humanoids need reflexive dodges rather than giant leaps?
sections.summary: When objects approach quickly from close range, conventional path planning or footstep adjustments are simply too slow. BARE proposes a reflexive control framework that exploits the high degrees of freedom in humanoids to evade obstacles through localized bodily adjustments rather than large-scale whole-body maneuvers.
sections.details:
When deploying humanoid robots in the real world, collisions with flying objects or sudden obstacles can immediately interrupt tasks, cause falls, or damage hardware—making avoidance a top priority. Prior work has explored visual path planning, real-time footstep generation, and online gait adaptation.

However, when an object flies in at high speed from close range, computational planning delays and actuator response limits make it impossible to simply walk away in time. Such urgent situations demand an ability to evade unconsciously and reflexively, just like humans do. Recently, reinforcement learning has enabled successful reflexive evasion in quadruped robots (such as REBot), but these approaches primarily rely on large whole-body maneuvers like leaping or stepping back.

Attempting similar whole-body maneuvers with a humanoid severely complicates ground reaction forces and balance control, making falls much more likely. Moreover, in confined spaces, large movements risk collisions with surrounding walls or furniture. In contrast, humanoids possess a major advantage: high joint articulation. Performing local evasive motions—such as quickly pulling back an arm, lifting one leg, or crouching slightly—requires neither large base displacement nor large surrounding clearance, saving both space and execution time.

Nonetheless, even localized movements cause drastic shifts in mass distribution and alter support foot conditions when arms or legs are swung rapidly. The fundamental challenge therefore becomes: how can a humanoid evade locally and rapidly while maintaining whole-body stability and returning to upright standing? BARE addresses this challenge by incorporating human evasive motions as motion priors to achieve both whole-body coordination and local evasion.

sections.heading: From motion imitation to reflexive evasion: prior approaches and where BARE stands
sections.summary: While human motion imitation and quadruped reflexive evasion have advanced, integrating localized evasion with whole-body balance using humanoid articulation remained unexplored. BARE bridges this gap by linking human motion priors with a risk-guided adaptation mechanism.
sections.details:
This work builds on two primary research threads: humanoid motion learning and dynamic obstacle avoidance.

First, in motion learning, reinforcement-learning-based motion tracking techniques like DeepMimic and AMP have advanced rapidly. Recent methods such as H2O and BeyondMimic have applied rich human motion data to complex tasks like whole-body teleoperation, parkour, and table tennis. These motion priors provide powerful inductive biases for generating human-like coordinated movement.

Second, in safe navigation, techniques like FootstepNet and Model Predictive Control (MPC) have been proposed to navigate around dynamic obstacles. However, because these rely fundamentally on modifying walking paths, their response times are insufficient against high-speed threats at close range.

Consequently, reflexive evasion has gained attention. Drones have used event cameras for ultra-fast evasion, while quadruped robots have adopted RL frameworks like REBot, APREBot, and UEREBot to trigger jumps or lateral steps. However, these quadruped methods depend on large whole-body displacements, leaving the humanoid approach of dodging in place using rich multi-joint articulation largely unaddressed. BARE fills this void by coupling a human evasive motion library with link-level collision risk estimation to realize flexible, humanoid-specific evasion.

sections.heading: Problem formulation: how to mathematically define collision-free whole-body stability
sections.summary: The robot begins from a static standing posture facing spherical obstacles approaching at high speeds from various directions and heights. The task is defined as successfully avoiding contact across all links primarily through local joint adjustments, while maintaining balance and returning to standing both during and after evasion.
sections.details:
Let us examine the problem formulation. The robot has $n$ actuated joints and its state $x_t$ comprises the base position, orientation, linear velocity, angular velocity, and joint positions and velocities. The obstacle is approximated as a sphere $o_t = (p_t^O, v_t^O, r^O)$ with position, velocity, and radius.

A key element is the definition of clearance. Letting $\mathcal{J}$ denote the set of all robot links and $\mathcal{B}_j(x_t)$ the spatial volume occupied by link $j$, the signed surface clearance to the obstacle is defined as $d_j(t)$. The whole-body minimum clearance is then $d_{\min}(t) = \min_{j\in\mathcal{J}} d_j(t)$. A positive value indicates clearance, zero indicates contact, and a negative value indicates penetration. Crucially, dodging the threatened region only to have the obstacle strike another link still counts as a collision. Therefore, the robot must maintain $d_{\min}(t) > 0$ across all links at all times.

The task sequence begins with the robot in an upright stance. Upon detecting an approaching obstacle, it reflexively transitions into an evasive posture, and once the threat passes, it promptly returns to a stable standing posture. Three criteria define success: no contact with the obstacle during its passage, no falling or termination during the evasion and recovery phases, and a stable return to a static upright stance after the obstacle has cleared.

captions.F2: Overall task flow. When an object approaches from the right and the risk exceeds threshold $\eta$, the robot quickly transitions from an upright stance to an evasive posture (here, a crouch), and smoothly returns to upright standing after the object passes.

sections.heading: BARE architecture: risk-guided motion selection, phase adaptation, and residual RL
sections.summary: An optimal reference motion is selected from a library built from human evasion videos based on link-level risk. An RL-based phase adapter stretches or compresses motion timing according to obstacle arrival time, while a residual policy generates joint commands that preserve whole-body balance.
sections.details:
BARE consists of two main tiers: a risk-guided motion adapter and a reflexive evasion policy.

### IV-A & IV-B Risk-Guided Motion Adapter
First, an offline motion library $\mathcal{M} = \{\xi_k\}$ retargeted for the humanoid is constructed from human evasion videos using pose estimation (GVHMR) and motion retargeting (GMR). This library includes both "local evasion" (raising arms, lifting legs, crouching) and "whole-body maneuvers" (lateral steps, stepping back).

Online, links are approximated by bounding spheres. Assuming constant linear velocity, the time to closest approach $\tau_{j,t}^*$ and the corresponding clearance are computed analytically from relative position $a_{j,t}$ and velocity $b_{j,t}$. These values are passed through a sigmoid function to compute the collision risk $\rho_{j,t}$ for each link. When the maximum risk across the body $\rho_t^{\max}$ exceeds a threshold $\eta$, evasion is triggered.

Motion selection is rule-based. If a local evasive motion covers the high-risk link set, it is selected as a candidate; otherwise, whole-body maneuvers are considered. Taking the approach direction into account, a single reference motion is determined.

Simply playing back the chosen reference motion cannot handle varying approach speeds. This is where "Ref. Phase Adaptation" comes in. An RL-trained policy $\mathcal{T}_\psi$ outputs a phase rate scaling factor $s_t$ based on obstacle approach status. This temporal adaptation accelerates the motion for ultra-fast objects so the robot reaches the evasive posture before contact, or slows it down for slower objects to time the dodge appropriately.

### IV-C Reflexive Evasion Policy
While the adapted reference motion provides an ideal guide, real-world joint delays and dynamics discrepancies must be compensated. A residual RL framework bridges this gap. The policy $\pi_\theta$ outputs joint adjustments $\delta q_t$, which are added to the reference joint positions $\bar{q}_t$:
$$u_t = \bar{q}_t + \beta (w_t \odot \delta q_t)$$
Here, $w_t$ is a binary mask that focuses corrections onto the joints intended to move in the reference motion. This prevents irrelevant joints from flailing while maintaining coordinated balance through the supporting legs and trunk.

The reward function incorporates collision avoidance penalties (contact and insufficient clearance), reference motion tracking terms, locality rewards (penalizing the number of moving joints, base displacement, and power consumption), and regularization terms to prevent falls and joint limit violations. Training is conducted efficiently via PPO using a combination of staged learning and joint optimization.

captions.F3: Overall BARE system architecture. The link-level risk estimator on the left computes danger levels, while the motion selection module on the top right chooses a reference motion from the human motion library. The phase adaptation module in the center modulates the progression speed $s_t$, and the reflexive evasion policy at the bottom adds residual corrections to send torque/position commands to the robot simulator.

sections.heading: Simulation evaluation: fast evasion success with low energy and minimal displacement
sections.summary: Using Unitree G1 in a MuJoCo simulation environment, performance was evaluated across varying obstacle arrival times and angles. BARE outperformed baseline methods in avoidance success rate while significantly reducing base movement distance and peak power consumption.
sections.details:
Simulation experiments evaluated evasion performance on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 against objects approaching from all 360-degree directions and diverse heights. Trials were categorized by obstacle arrival time $T_{\mathrm{arr}}$ into short (0.10–0.50 s), medium (0.50–1.50 s), and long (1.50–3.00 s) regimes.

BARE was compared against two baselines: "REBot (G1 adapted)," an RL-based evasion method without reference motions, and "FootstepNet (G1 adapted)," a footstep-planning navigation approach. Metrics included Avoidance Success Rate (ASR), Average Movement Distance of the base on successful trials (AMD), and Peak Total Power (PTP).

### Key Findings
In terms of ASR, BARE achieved 0.12 in the short regime, 0.53 in the medium regime, and 0.83 in the long regime, outperforming FootstepNet (0.08 / 0.31 / 0.61) and REBot (0.10 / 0.39 / 0.64) across all intervals. With 0.5 seconds or more of warning, BARE reliably evaded and recovered from 50% to over 80% of incoming attacks.

Even more striking were the compactness and energy efficiency of the motions. While REBot took large steps with base displacements (AMD) of 0.7–0.8 m or more, BARE maintained an AMD of just 0.14–0.16 m. Peak total power (PTP) for BARE remained between 0.33 and 0.42 kW, roughly half that of baselines (REBot exceeded 0.8 kW). These results demonstrate that swift, compact dodges minimize disruption in confined spaces while substantially reducing actuator strain.

### Ablation Study Insights
Ablation experiments further validated individual components. When motion selection was replaced with random choice (w/o selection), ASR dropped catastrophically to 0.02–0.12, confirming that choosing motions matching threatened body parts is essential. Fixing the phase rate without adaptation (w/o phase) caused the long-regime ASR to fall to 0.42, showing the necessity of temporally stretching motions to incoming speeds. Removing locality rewards (w/o locality) also degraded success (0.08 / 0.46 / 0.72), verifying that suppressing unnecessary joint movements directly aids whole-body balance.

captions.F5: Comparison results against baselines. (a) Distribution of movement distance (AMD) vs. peak power (PTP) on successful trials; BARE (green) concentrates in the low-movement, low-power region at the bottom left. (b) Avoidance success rate (ASR) across arrival times, showing BARE consistently on top. (c) Radar chart of success rates across 8 horizontal attack directions.

sections.heading: Real-world tests: a physical Unitree G1 dodges thrusts and kicks in real time
sections.summary: BARE was deployed on a physical Unitree G1 with obstacles tracked via motion capture. Against dynamic human-administered attacks including thrusts, low sweeps, and kicks, the robot achieved a 57% evasion success rate in the real world.
sections.details:
To validate practical efficacy, real-world experiments were conducted on an actual Unitree G1. An OptiTrack motion capture system tracked marker-equipped obstacles, converting position and velocity measurements into the robot base frame in real time.

An experimenter launched sudden attacks from diverse heights and directions, including thrusts and sweeps using a stick with a ball attached to its tip, kicks, thrown frisbee-like discs, and horizontal fist sweeps.

Starting from an upright stance, the robot instantly lowered its body, raised its arm, or lifted a leg as an attack neared, evading contact and smoothly returning to a stable standing posture once the threat passed. Across all real-world test trials, the robot achieved an overall evasion success rate of 57%.

While this is lower than simulation performance (53–83% in medium-to-long regimes), the authors attribute the gap to sensing, communication, and control latencies, delayed actuator torque responses on the physical hardware, and friction uncertainties in ground contact dynamics. Even so, successfully demonstrating such agile, stable reflexive evasion on a physical humanoid without pre-planned trajectories represents a significant milestone.

captions.F6: Evasion sequences on the real Unitree G1 robot. Top row (a): crouching to evade a head-level attack. Middle row (b): leaning back to dodge a horizontal sweep at the torso. Bottom row (c): lifting a leg to avoid a stick sweeping at foot level.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: how humanoid body agility opens the door to safe coexistence
sections.summary: BARE blends human motion priors with risk-adaptive mechanisms to harmonize local evasion and fall prevention in humanoids. Next steps include migrating from external motion capture to onboard sensors and extending evasion to uneven terrain.
sections.details:
This paper presented BARE, a framework enabling humanoid robots in confined spaces to evade sudden threats through localized bodily adjustments rather than relying on quadruped-like large leaps, all while maintaining balance.

The complete pipeline—link-level geometric risk estimation, motion library selection grounded in human priors, temporal phase adaptation, and whole-body coordination via residual reinforcement learning—proved highly effective in both simulation and physical robot experiments.

Limitations remain to be addressed. The primary constraint is the physical setup's reliance on external motion capture for obstacle tracking. Future iterations will aim to integrate onboard depth or event cameras for active perception, enabling self-contained sensing. Furthermore, the current setup assumes static standing on flat ground; extending evasive capabilities to uneven terrain, during walking, or under constrained support bases remains an important direction for future research.

takeaways: Humanoid obstacle avoidance does not always require stepping or leaping away; localized movements like pulling back an arm, lifting a leg, or crouching offer significant advantages in time and spatial clearance.
Selecting reference motions from a human evasive library based on threatened body links and using RL to scale playback phase to obstacle speed are critical to high evasion success.
Using residual RL with a joint mask focused on target limbs allows targeted local evasion without compromising whole-body balance.
limitations: Physical experiments rely on an external motion capture system (OptiTrack) to track obstacle positions and velocities, falling short of fully autonomous onboard sensing.
Under extremely short arrival times (under 0.5 seconds), physical actuator response limits lead to a marked drop in evasion success rates.
The approach is currently evaluated only from a static upright stance on flat ground, leaving stability during walking locomotion or on uneven, stepped terrain unverified.
